Know Your Rights Under the FTC Funeral Rule Every funeral home in New Mexico must comply with the Federal Trade Commission's Funeral Rule, which protects consumers nationwide. State oversight sits with the New Mexico Board of Funeral Services in the Regulation and Licensing Department, which licenses and regulates funeral directors, funeral homes and crematoriums; its stated first duty is to protect the public in the handling and care of the dead.
What you pay for a funeral in New Mexico

Part of every New Mexico quote is the building itself. Board rules make a licensed establishment keep a chapel of at least 600 square feet seating 60 or more, a casket display room of at least 450 square feet showing no fewer than 12 adult caskets or models (with the caskets warehoused within 50 miles), and refrigeration with at least 12 and one-half cubic feet per body (16.64.4.8 NMAC). Those fixed costs, plus local competition and land prices, are why Mountain pricing still sits below the US median of $8,300 yet a city chapel and a small-town one in New Mexico can quote 10-30% apart.

The VA burial allowance is claimed by whoever paid the bill, using Form 21P-530EZ; for a non-service-connected death on or after October 1, 2026 it reaches $1,032 toward burial and another $1,032 toward a plot. A family that skips the chapel entirely can use a New Mexico direct disposer, who must hand over a written statement first saying it cannot hold rites or provide facilities for them and allows no viewing except to identify the body (16.64.9.8 NMAC). Who qualifies is set out in our veteran burial benefits guide.

It is not the South Dakota Funeral Association, which is a trade group that promotes the profession.
What you pay for a funeral in South Dakota

A South Dakota funeral bill is shaped by a short statute list as much as by the market. Every funeral establishment has to be run by a licensed manager (SDCL 36-19-30) and the State Board of Funeral Service inspects each one at least once every three years (SDCL 36-19-31). Within those rules, Midwest pricing generally lands under the US median of $8,300, and a Sioux Falls or Rapid City home can price 10-30% away from a rural South Dakota one.
For a South Dakota veteran

South Dakota law expects every body to be decently buried within a reasonable time (SDCL 34-26-15); a person charged with that duty who neglects it commits a Class 1 misdemeanor and owes whoever steps in treble the burial expense (SDCL 34-26-18). For a veteran, the payer files VA Form 21P-530EZ: up to $1,032 for burial plus $1,032 for a plot when a non-service-connected death falls on or after October 1, 2026. Eligibility details for South Dakota families are in our veteran burial benefits guide.

Under Idaho Code § 54-1139, a person who funds a prearranged funeral plan can put cremation instructions in it and sign the cremation authorization form ahead of time. Anything the plan does not clearly cover falls back to the next-of-kin order in § 54-1142, and simply owning a burial plot does not count as a prearranged plan.
In short, Idaho has no fixed minimum waiting period

Idaho sets no minimum waiting period, but the paperwork has its own steps. Under Idaho Code § 39-268, the mortician who first takes charge of the body reports to the district registrar within 24 hours, and whoever signs the death certificate authorizes final disposition. For a cremation, the coroner must also give an additional authorization, and the crematory still needs a signed authorization from the next of kin or designated agent. For the funeral-director question and who takes complaints, see the cremation rules and help section lower on this page.
cremation-costs-missouri.html: Get the Missouri provider's General Price List

Missouri's right-of-sepulcher law, RSMo § 194.119, sets who may authorize a cremation: first an attorney in fact given that right in a durable power of attorney, then the person a service member who died on active duty named on DD Form 93, then the spouse, a child, a parent, a sibling and the next nearest relative. After them come a friend who agrees to pay and, last, the county coroner or medical examiner.
In short, Missouri has no fixed minimum waiting period

Missouri sets no fixed minimum waiting period, but it does set out who may decide. Under RSMo § 194.119, anyone who wants to make the arrangements must first notify a person with a higher claim, and that person waives the right by not objecting within 48 hours of being notified in person or by written notice with delivery confirmation. No Missouri cremation starts until the crematory holds that signed authorization from whoever holds the decision under § 194.119, a cremation permit and the death certificate. Funeral-director requirements and the complaint office are in the rules and help section below.

After that the decision passes to a majority of the surviving children, then the parents, then a majority of the siblings; fewer than half of the children may act only after reasonable efforts to notify the rest and with no known opposition from a majority.

Older municipal and religious cemeteries in Rhode Island were often set up on land donated or endowed long ago, and their pricing can still reflect that. A 15-minute longer drive to one of these can cut $1,760 or more off your cemetery bill.

cremation-costs-mississippi.html: The licensing office for cremation providers in Mississippi

The licensing office for cremation providers in Mississippi is the Mississippi State Board of Funeral Service; its number is 601-932-1973. The board has its office at 3010 Lakeland Cove, Suite W, in Flowood, and its fax number is 601-932-1901.
Before a Mississippi body can be cremated, a medical examiner

Before a Mississippi body can be cremated, a medical examiner has to certify that he has looked into the cause and manner of death and sees no need for further examination. The examiner or a deputy may charge the applicant $25 for that certificate, unless the county has already paid for a written death investigation report (Miss. Code Ann. § 41-61-69(2); checked October 29, 2026). Consent is the other gate. No Mississippi funeral home or crematory may cremate without prior written or oral consent from the next of kin or authorized agent, in the priority order of § 73-11-58, and when consent is given by phone the home must write down who gave it, how that person is related, the date and time, and who took the call (Miss. Code Ann. § 73-11-73). A family can ask for a copy of that record alongside the signed contract.
cremation-costs-vermont.html: In short, Vermont sets a 24-hour minimum before cremation

In short, Vermont sets a 24-hour minimum before cremation, and the crematory also needs the death certificate, a cremation permit and a signed authorization from the next of kin or designated agent. Get the Vermont provider's General Price List

Paying ahead for a Vermont cremation? State law requires the prepaid contract to be in writing and to itemize the services and merchandise; you can move it to another funeral director, in Vermont or elsewhere, for a transfer fee capped at five percent of the principal (26 V.S.A. § 1273; 26 V.S.A. § 1274).
Vermont is not among the nine states

Families need no funeral director under Vermont law (the Funeral Consumers Alliance agrees, leaving Vermont off its nine-state list), yet every funeral establishment and disposition facility, crematories included, must be inspected at least once every two years (26 V.S.A. § 1213), and none will start without the death certificate, the cremation permit and the next of kin's signed authorization.
A Vermont provider offering direct cremation must let you use

Skip the casket for a Vermont direct cremation: the FTC Funeral Rule (16 CFR 453.3(b)) entitles you to an unfinished wood box or other alternative container, and Vermont lists cremation alongside earth burial, entombment and natural organic reduction as a lawful permanent disposition (18 V.S.A. § 5319).
In Vermont you do not have to buy the urn from the crematory

An urn bought elsewhere is fine: the FTC Funeral Rule lets Vermont families supply their own, and a refusal by a funeral home or crematory here is a matter for the VT Office of Professional Regulation.
Before signing, ask the Vermont provider when the ashes will be ready

Get answers in writing first from the Vermont provider: the date the ashes will be ready, how they come back to you, and whether a certified copy of the death certificate is in the price. For a prepaid plan, the contract must also say whether it is revocable or irrevocable (26 V.S.A. § 1273).
cremation-costs-arizona.html: Yes. An Arizona family can hold a viewing or service before cremation

Yes. An Arizona family can hold a viewing or service before cremation, and many providers rent a casket for it. Plan the date around the law: Arizona has no waiting period before cremation. The authorizing agent must give prior written consent and the medical examiner reviews the death certificate (A.R.S. § 32-1365.02). The authorizing agent is chosen by the priority order in A.R.S. § 36-831. When several people share the same rank, any one of them may sign unless another objects, and then a majority of those reasonably available decides; if no one is willing or able to pay, the county public fiduciary may order the cremation (A.R.S. § 32-1365.02).
The Funeral Consumers Alliance does not list Arizona

The Funeral Consumers Alliance does not list Arizona among the nine states that restrict family-directed care, so an Arizona family may deal with a crematory directly after the cremation permit is issued. There is no waiting period before cremation in Arizona. Arizona also licenses alkaline hydrolysis, which some providers sell as water cremation. The law defines it as reducing the body with water, alkaline chemicals, heat and pressure, and no one may run or even advertise a hydrolysis facility without a separate state license (A.R.S. § 32-1301, § 32-1341). If one is offered, ask for that license and compare its price with flame cremation line by line. A second rule helps when relatives are hard to reach: if the person with the right to authorize cannot be contacted, or will not make arrangements within 15 days of the provider's first contact, the provider may treat that person as unavailable and take consent from the next person in line (A.R.S. § 32-1365.02).
cremation-costs-oregon.html: Crematories and the funeral homes that sell cremation in Oregon

Crematories and the funeral homes that sell cremation in Oregon answer to the Oregon Mortuary and Cemetery Board (971-673-1500). The board has eleven volunteer members appointed by the Governor, seven from the death care industry and four from the public, and it pays its way through licensing, examination and death record filing fees.
Direct cremation, with no service, and cremation with a memorial

Direct cremation, with no service, and cremation with a memorial or viewing are the usual choices. Oregon law also recognizes alkaline hydrolysis, or water cremation, defining it as a form of reduction done in a licensed hydrolysis facility (ORS 97.010); ask a provider whether it offers it and how the price compares with flame cremation. With no minimum waiting period, the paperwork sets the timing, and the permit rules are under Timing and permits below. Since the 2021 session Oregon has also allowed natural organic reduction, the contained, accelerated conversion of a body to soil that is often called human composting (HB 2574). The Mortuary and Cemetery Board says hydrolysis and natural organic reduction are the only alternatives it has approved by rule, and a firm offering either must hold an alternative disposition facility license (Oregon Mortuary and Cemetery Board). Fewer Oregon firms sell these than sell flame cremation, so ask for the license number and a written price before choosing one.

The licensing office for cremation providers in Texas is the Texas Funeral Service Commission; its number is 512-936-2474. R.S. 37:831, licenses crematory authorities and retort operators as well as funeral homes; its count on September 16, 2026 was 48 crematory authorities and 427 funeral establishments.
cremation-costs-north-carolina.html: What the law says about timing

What the law says about timing: North Carolina bars cremation within 24 hours after death, and a medical examiner must certify that no further examination is needed (N.C.G.S. 90-210.129, 130A-388). The same statute gives relatives and their invitees access to the crematory area, subject to the crematory's safety rules, and it requires remains to be kept at 40 degrees Fahrenheit or colder unless the cremation will begin within 24 hours of the crematory taking custody.
burial-costs-new-mexico.html: For New Mexico veterans, the plot and marker

For New Mexico veterans, the plot and marker in a national cemetery are free, which can remove thousands from a burial bill. In New Mexico, VA national cemeteries accepting burials: Fort Bayard National Cemetery (505-988-6400); Santa Fe National Cemetery (505-988-6400); state veterans cemeteries: Angel Fire State Veterans Cemetery (505-225-4341); Fort Stanton State Veterans Cemetery (505-205-6707); Gallup State Veterans Cemetery (575-921-3494) (source: VA National Cemetery Administration). The New Mexico Department of Veterans Services, which runs these cemeteries, also operates a fourth, Taos State Veterans Cemetery in Ranchos de Taos (505-470-3065), and lists its own numbers for Fort Stanton (505-383-4381) and Gallup (505-905-9770).
New Mexico skips the permit for most burials

New Mexico skips the permit for most burials. When a death happens in the state and a licensed funeral service practitioner or direct disposer handles a burial in the state, no burial-transit permit is needed. A permit from the state or a local registrar is required when the body leaves New Mexico or when someone other than those licensees, such as the family itself, carries out the burial (NMSA § 24-14-23; checked October 29, 2026). Timing matters as well. If burial will not happen within 24 hours of death, the body must be embalmed or refrigerated (NMSA § 61-32-20), and the board's rules set refrigeration at 40°F or colder (16.64.4 NMAC). Embalming is not otherwise required, so a family planning a closed-casket burial within a few days can ask the funeral home to price refrigeration instead.
burial-costs-utah.html: For Utah veterans, the plot and marker

For Utah veterans, the plot and marker in a national cemetery are free, which can remove thousands from a burial bill. In Utah, VA national cemeteries accepting burials: Southern Utah National Cemetery (435-267-2710); state veterans cemetery: Utah Veterans Cemetery and Memorial Park (801-254-9036) (source: VA National Cemetery Administration). Southern Utah National Cemetery is in Cedar City, and the state-run Utah Veterans Cemetery and Memorial Park, in Bluffdale, is the closer option for families around Salt Lake City. The Utah Department of Veterans and Military Affairs reports VA grants of more than $16.5 million to add 1,400 columbarium niches at Bluffdale and to establish a new state veterans cemetery in Washington Terrace.
When a winter death means a spring burial in Utah

When a winter death means a spring burial in Utah, ask two things: whether the cemetery charges to keep the casket in its receiving vault, and whether the funeral home's price includes a second trip in spring. Interment seasons differ widely across the state, so ask each cemetery about its own. A family that can wait until spring may also have more time to compare monument quotes before the headstone is ordered. Vault rules are set cemetery by cemetery. Nephi's city cemeteries, for example, require a vault for every burial, made of concrete, steel, fiberglass or another material the sexton approves, with no wood in any permanent part (Nephi City cemetery policies). The same policy bans artificial flowers on graves from April 1 to November 1 apart from listed holidays, which is worth knowing before ordering a winter arrangement.
burial-costs-wyoming.html: Eligible Wyoming veterans get a grave

Eligible Wyoming veterans get a grave, opening and closing, a liner and a headstone at no cost in a national cemetery. In Wyoming, VA national cemeteries accepting burials: Cheyenne National Cemetery (307-778-7316); state veterans cemetery: Oregon Trail State Veterans Cemetery (307-235-6673) (source: VA National Cemetery Administration). Cheyenne National Cemetery is in the state's southeast corner, and the Oregon Trail State Veterans Cemetery is in Evansville, next to Casper. The Wyoming Veterans Commission was founded in 1981 to receive the federal funding that established the Evansville cemetery, and it still oversees it.
burial-costs-south-dakota.html: Eligible South Dakota veterans get a grave

Eligible South Dakota veterans get a grave, opening and closing, a liner and a headstone at no cost in a national cemetery. In South Dakota, VA national cemeteries accepting burials: Black Hills National Cemetery (605-347-3830); state and tribal veterans cemeteries: South Dakota Veterans Cemetery (605-277-8094); Akicita Owicahe Lakota Freedom Veterans Cemetery (tribal, 605-455-1497); Sicangu Akicita Owicahe Veterans Cemetery (tribal, 605-259-3044); Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate Veterans Cemetery (tribal, 605-698-3388) (source: VA National Cemetery Administration). The Sicangu Akicita Owicahe Veterans Cemetery number comes from the tribe's office directory. The South Dakota Veterans Cemetery was dedicated on Memorial Day 2021 and held its first burials on June 4 that year; to arrange one, the family gives the cemetery the DD214 or enough service details for it to confirm eligibility.
Because the Funeral Consumers Alliance does not count South Dakota

South Dakota is not one of the nine states the Funeral Consumers Alliance lists as requiring a funeral director, so a family may arrange the burial itself once it holds the burial permit and follows the cemetery's grave rules.
If the person served, ask Black Hills National Cemetery
Black Hills National Cemetery can tell a veteran's family which papers to bring; expect the DD214 discharge record to be first on the list.
Report a funeral home that misprices a burial to the board at 605-642-1600
If a South Dakota funeral home gets its burial prices wrong, the state board takes complaints at 605-642-1600.
burial-costs-north-carolina.html: For a license check or complaint about a funeral home arranging a burial in North Carolina

For a license check or complaint about a funeral home arranging a burial in North Carolina, call the North Carolina Board of Funeral Service at 919-733-9380; North Carolina cemeteries can have a separate regulator. For most cemeteries that regulator is the N.C. Cemetery Commission, which supervises cemeteries, their sales organizations and brokers, and preneed cemetery salespeople under Chapter 65, Article 9; cemeteries run by churches or government agencies fall outside that law.
burial-costs-vermont.html: For a license check or complaint about a funeral home arranging a burial in Vermont

For a license check or complaint about a funeral home arranging a burial in Vermont, call the Vermont Office of Professional Regulation at 802-828-1188; Vermont cemeteries can have a separate regulator. Vermont cemetery law sits in Title 18, Chapter 121. Under 18 V.S.A. § 5313, a cemetery's record of where remains are permanently placed must be open to the public at all reasonable times, and § 5323 lets a natural burial ground locate graves by mapping, surveying or GPS instead of a standard plat.
burial-costs-wisconsin.html: The Wisconsin Department of Safety and Professional Services

The Wisconsin Department of Safety and Professional Services (608-266-2112) licenses the funeral homes that arrange burials in Wisconsin. It can also tell you which Wisconsin office handles cemetery complaints. Cemeteries themselves come under the Cemetery Board housed at DSPS, whose six members, four representing licensed cemetery authorities and two from the public, are appointed by the Governor for four-year terms.
cremation-costs-virginia.html: Virginia sets no minimum number of hours, but one step is easy to overlook: no one who died in the state may be cremated until a medical examiner has decided the death needs no further medicolegal inquiry and has signed a certificate on a form from the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (Va. Code § 32.1-309.3). That applies whatever the cause and manner of death, and the examiner's fee, capped by the Board of Health, is paid by whoever applies. For the exact Virginia citation, the funeral-director question and who takes complaints, see the cremation rules and help section lower on this page.
cremation-costs-minnesota.html: Minnesota sets deadlines rather than a wait. A body has to reach final disposition within 14 calendar days of death or release by the coroner or medical examiner, and if that will take more than 72 hours it must be embalmed, refrigerated or packed in dry ice; refrigeration is capped at 14 days and dry ice at four (Minn. Stat. § 149A.94). Once a crematory accepts custody, it has 24 hours to carry out the cremation (Minn. Stat. § 149A.95). The statute behind the Minnesota timing rule, whether a funeral director must be involved, and the licensing board's phone number are listed in the cremation rules section further down this page.
cremation-costs-delaware.html: Delaware has no waiting clock in its funeral law, but it does insist on identification: unless the person was already identified, the remains cannot be cremated until the next of kin, the person authorized to make the arrangements, or the medical examiner has identified them. The body must also travel to the crematory in a rigid, leak-resistant container of combustible material, and metal or polyethylene does not qualify (24 Del. C. § 3121). For the exact Delaware citation, the funeral-director question and who takes complaints, see the cremation rules and help section lower on this page.
cremation-costs-west-virginia.html: West Virginia law does not make families wait a set number of hours. What it spells out is who decides: before a body goes to a funeral director or crematory operator, the decedent's own wishes in a will, advance directive or preneed contract come first, then a surviving spouse (unless a divorce petition was pending), then someone the decedent named in a signed, notarized writing, and only after that the next of kin. Nobody may hold that designation for more than one nonrelative at a time (W. Va. Code § 30-6-22). For the exact West Virginia citation, the funeral-director question and who takes complaints, see the cremation rules and help section lower on this page.
The Funeral Consumers Alliance does not count West Virginia

The Funeral Consumers Alliance does not count West Virginia among the nine states that require a funeral director. Even so, no crematory in the state will start without the death certificate, the cremation permit and the next of kin's signed authorization. There is no waiting period; what the law requires is written next-of-kin permission and a cremation permit from a medical examiner or coroner (W. Va. Code 30-6-21). If no one collects the ashes, the funeral board sets a slow timetable: 60 days after the cremation the provider must write by certified mail to the person due to receive them, write again 30 days later, and warn that it may dispose of them if they are still unclaimed 90 days after that (WV Board of Funeral Service Examiners). At the arrangement conference the funeral home must also tell the family in writing that unclaimed remains may go into a common grave and may not be recoverable later (W. Va. Code R. § 6-1-24).
cremation-costs-south-carolina.html: About 45% of South Carolina deaths now end in cremation, still under the national rate, and the savings against a traditional burial usually run $5,100 or more. You can settle the question yourself in advance: state law lets a person sign a cremation authorization form for their own cremation, revocable at any time by written notice to both the funeral home and the crematory, and whoever holds that form at death must see that its instructions are followed (S.C. Code § 32-8-315).
In South Carolina the person who arranges a cremation

In South Carolina the person who arranges a cremation must get the permit from the coroner or medical examiner of the county where the death happened. Wilfully skipping it is a misdemeanor (S.C. Code § 17-5-600). Coroners set their own charges, so the price varies by county. Richland County takes requests online only, and they must include the signed death certificate, the burial-removal-transit permit and the signed cremation authorization. The office emails the permit back and charges $20 (Richland County Coroner's Office; checked October 29, 2026). Two later rules protect the family once the form is signed. The agent who signed the cremation authorization can cancel it in writing within 12 hours, and the funeral home and crematory must honor that. If the form names no grave, niche or scattering area, the crematory may hold the ashes for 30 days, then return them, and may dispose of them after 60 days if no arrangements have been made (S.C. Code § 32-8-325).
funeral-costs-north-dakota.html: What you pay for a funeral in North Dakota

North Dakota funeral prices are usually below the US median of $8,300, and city and rural quotes can differ by 10-30%. Every funeral home is overseen by a small board: the state health officer or a designee plus three governor-appointed embalmers, each with at least three years of practice in North Dakota. Each place of business needs its own establishment license, a crematorium needs an annual license costing no more than $100, and the board writes the rules for what happens to cremated remains a funeral home is left holding when no one claims them (N.D.C.C. ch. 43-10).
funeral-costs-iowa.html: What you pay for a funeral in Iowa

Iowa quotes generally come in under the $8,300 national median, with metro and rural homes often 10-30% apart. Before comparing them, settle who can sign. Iowa lets an adult name a designee, and an alternate, in a written declaration; without one, control passes to a spouse who was not legally separated, then a majority of the surviving children, then the parents, then a majority of the grandchildren, then of the siblings, then of the grandparents (Iowa Code § 144C.5).
funeral-costs-michigan.html: What you pay for a funeral in Michigan

Michigan prices sit near the middle of the country, below the $8,300 national median in many towns, and metro quotes can run 10-30% above rural ones. Michigan also lets anyone 18 or older of sound mind name a "funeral representative" in a dated, signed writing; that person can decide on funeral arrangements and cremation and may collect the cremated remains right after the cremation. Whoever decides, the handling of the body must be supervised by someone licensed in mortuary science (MCL 700.3206).
funeral-costs-nebraska.html: What you pay for a funeral in Nebraska

A Nebraska funeral usually costs less than the US median of $8,300, and quotes in the larger cities can be 10-30% higher than small-town ones. Families sometimes lose time arguing over who signs. Nebraska settles it: an adult can direct their own arrangements through a will, a pre-need contract, or an affidavit sworn before a notary that names a person to control the remains, and otherwise the right goes to the surviving spouse and then to the children, a majority of them deciding (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 30-2223).
funeral-costs-ohio.html: NFDA puts the 2023 national median at $8,300 for a funeral with viewing and burial and $6,280 with cremation; set those beside the Ohio table here, then collect several price lists, because single homes stray far from any average. If you are weighing a prepaid plan, Ohio allows only a licensed funeral director to sell a preneed contract that includes funeral services (R.C. 4717.31). The holder of the money, or the seller, must also check on the beneficiary in the year they turn 105, and if no one can confirm they are alive the funds go to the state's unclaimed funds program (R.C. 4717.311).
funeral-costs-oregon.html: Direct cremation, about $1,900 in Oregon, is the cheapest route, and conservation burial grounds or hybrid sections of a cemetery often cost 30-50% less than a traditional plot. Before anyone prepays, know that Oregon treats your own written directions seriously: an adult can set the manner of disposition in a signed document or by prearranging with a licensed funeral service practitioner, and prepaid or filed arrangements generally cannot be cancelled or substantially revised later. Without such directions, the spouse decides first, then adult children, then a parent (ORS 97.130). Asking for General Price Lists from three providers is still the simplest way to compare.
funeral-costs-new-hampshire.html: Direct cremation runs about $2,100 in New Hampshire, and municipal, Catholic and Jewish cemeteries often cost at least $1,000 less than private memorial parks. A death between December and March can bring a frozen-ground charge, so ask for it in writing. If you buy ahead, New Hampshire requires any prearranged contract funded through a trust, insurance policy or annuity to be in writing and to list the seller's name, address and phone number and the purchaser's name and address, plus the beneficiary's if that is someone else (RSA 325:46-a). Comparing three General Price Lists still saves the most.

funeral-costs-minnesota.html: The biggest lever is comparison shopping

cremation-costs-wisconsin.html: Wisconsin keeps a 48-hour minimum before cremation, and the details in Wis. Stat. ch. 440, subch. VII go further than most states. A crematory may not turn remains away only because they arrive without a casket or without embalming (§440.77). The container can be any combustible, leak-resistant and rigid box, and if the authorization form lists a viewing, the cremation cannot start before that date and time (§440.78). An authorization can be revoked in writing (§440.76). Ashes left unclaimed may be disposed of no sooner than 30 days after cremation, and particles must first be reduced to ⅛ inch or less (§440.80).
cremation-costs-utah.html: Scattering ashes on public land in Utah

Utah's own rule for scattering sits in Utah Code 58-9-611: cremated remains may be scattered over uninhabited public land, the sea or other waterways, and on private land only with the owner's written consent. Before scattering, the remains must be reduced to particles of ⅛ inch or less and taken out of their closed container. A funeral establishment releasing remains for scattering needs a receipt showing the cremation was filed with the local registrar. If nobody collects the remains within 60 days, the establishment may dispose of them by any lawful means except scattering. With a 42% state cremation rate, many Utah families plan an outdoor memorial; dedicated scattering services run $200-$800, while a family scatter is free apart from any land-agency permit.
funeral-costs-oklahoma.html: What you pay for a funeral in Oklahoma

Oklahoma law shapes the bill in one specific way. Under 59 O.S. §396.12b, every funeral must be carried out under the personal supervision of a licensed funeral director from the first call until interment, and embalming may only be done by a licensed embalmer. That rule does not apply to relatives by blood or marriage who handle a burial themselves, which leaves room for a family-directed service. Paid supervision is still the norm, so the quote you receive reflects local competition and facility costs. Oklahoma sits in the South, where pricing generally runs below the US median of $8,300, and metro and rural homes in the state often differ by 10-30%.
funeral-costs-rhode-island.html: Rhode Island's funeral statute, R.I. Gen. Laws §5-33.2-12, says remains may not be held longer than 48 hours unless they are embalmed or refrigerated, so a delayed service means paying for one or the other. Each establishment must name one funeral director of record, and licenses run to December 31. A separate section, §5-33.2-9, keeps cemetery operators out of funeral directing and bars a funeral home on or beside cemetery grounds, which keeps the two price lists separate. The FTC Funeral Rule still applies on top. Complaints go to the Rhode Island Department of Health, Board of Funeral Directing/Embalming (401-222-4998).

A crematory may cremate only one body at a time and may not commingle remains. None of this requires embalming, and the FTC Funeral Rule forbids a home from claiming it is required by law when it is not. For a license check or complaint, call the West Virginia Board of Funeral Service Examiners at 304-558-0302.

South Carolina writes price disclosure into S.C. Code §40-19-290. Before a casket is chosen, the funeral home must give full disclosure of its charges and name related expenses such as cemetery and florist costs. Statements about embalming must be truthful. Money paid for merchandise in advance is held in trust, and the Department of Consumer Affairs can investigate. burial-costs-maine.html: Maine sets out who decides on a burial in 22 M.R.S. §2843-A. Custody follows a fixed order: spouse, then domestic partner, then an adult child, then a parent and onward. An estranged spouse or partner loses that right, and if the person entitled to decide does not act within 4 days, custody passes to the next level. When no decision is made within 30 days, the funeral director may bury the body at their own expense, and remains abandoned for 15 days may be buried, cremated or reduced by natural organic reduction. Direct burial without embalming or a ceremony usually remains the cheapest burial line, and a VA national cemetery burial is free for eligible Maine veterans.
funeral-costs-nevada.html: Nevada keeps its rules on the dead in NRS chapter 451. NRS 451.020 requires burial or cremation within a reasonable time, and once a body is cremated the remains may be carried without a permit and disposed of in any manner. NRS 451.024 sets the order of who controls disposition, starting with a person the decedent named in writing. The FTC Funeral Rule adds the itemized General Price List and phone quotes. funeral-costs-illinois.html: The biggest lever is comparison shopping

Illinois requires a fixed place of business behind every license. Under 225 ILCS 41/10-5, a funeral director and embalmer must work from an establishment devoted to the care and preparation of the dead, and an intern may assist only under a licensee's immediate personal supervision. Comparing price lists from two or three providers often saves $1,000 or more. Township and county cemeteries often charge half what private ones do, and at $2,000, direct cremation is the lowest-cost choice in Illinois. Family-owned homes are still common across the state, and many post clearer prices than the chains.
burial-costs-oregon.html: Oregon protects a spouse's place in a family plot. Under ORS 97.570, the spouse of a plot owner has a vested right to be interred in a plot with more than one space, and ORS 97.580 says that right cannot be removed without the spouse's written consent; a divorce ends it. Check a deed before selling unused spaces. On the funeral side, direct burial without embalming or a viewing is usually the cheapest choice, and a home may not charge a fee if you bring your own casket. Eligible Oregon veterans pay nothing for a VA national cemetery burial.
burial-costs-washington.html: Washington lists four lawful outcomes in RCW 68.50.110. Remains must be buried or reduced by cremation, alkaline hydrolysis or natural organic reduction within a reasonable time. Under RCW 68.50.185, only one person's remains may be processed at a time unless written permission is given after disclosure, and a violation is a gross misdemeanor. Direct burial skips embalming and a viewing, so it usually prices lowest, and you can supply your own casket with no handling fee. Veterans who qualify can be laid to rest in a VA national cemetery at no charge.
burial-costs-new-hampshire.html: New Hampshire allows burial on private land, but RSA 289:3 sets distance rules: no new burial ground within 100 feet of a dwelling, school or store without the owner's consent, or within 50 feet of water or a state highway, unless local zoning says otherwise. For plots, RSA 290:24 passes ownership to a written designee or heirs, with the probate court settling disputes. Ask each cemetery for written prices.
cremation-costs-maine.html: Get the Maine provider's General Price List

Maine's 32 M.R.S. §1405 requires that remains reach the crematory in a casket or suitable container, and the crematory must label that container with the person's name. Ask the provider which container its direct cremation price includes, and whether transport and an urn are covered.
Cremation cannot take place in the first 48 hours

Cremation cannot take place in the first 48 hours after death unless a contagious disease caused it, and the medical examiner must certify the death first (32 M.R.S. § 1405). The same permit law now covers natural organic reduction, sometimes called human composting: the state registrar or a town clerk may issue a permit for it only after the medical examiner's certificate, as for cremation (22 M.R.S. § 2843). Where the medical examiner performed an autopsy, the report is free to the next of kin; other requesters pay $35 (Maine Office of Chief Medical Examiner).
funeral-costs-delaware.html: Compare the Delaware figures

Delaware keeps funeral homes and cemeteries apart. Under 24 Del. C. §3119, a licensee may not interfere with a family's free choice of funeral home, run a mortuary inside a cemetery, or take any fee or benefit from a cemetery, crematory or natural organic reduction facility. Compare Delaware quotes with the national median of $8,300 with viewing and burial, or $6,280 with cremation (NFDA 2023).

cremation-costs-ohio.html: Ohio keeps a 24-hour minimum before cremation, and its Revised Code chapter 4717 lets you settle the paperwork early. funeral-costs-missouri.html: Missouri requires a signed statement of charges. Under RSMo 333.145, before services are provided the funeral home must give a written statement, signed by both sides, listing the selected service price, each extra item, the cash advances and the payment method. A cash advance may be billed only at the net amount the home paid, and displayed merchandise must be price-marked. Hold quotes against the national median of $8,300 with viewing and burial, or $6,280 with cremation (NFDA 2023).
cremation-costs-kansas.html: Kansas families usually pick among direct cremation ($1,500), with no viewing or ceremony; cremation followed by a memorial service; and traditional cremation ($5,300), with a full funeral first. K.S.A. 65-1760 defines an alternative container as a combustible, closable, leak-resistant and rigid receptacle other than a casket.
funeral-costs-vermont.html: The FTC Funeral Rule bars a Vermont

Vermont allows natural burial grounds under 18 V.S.A. §5323, which exempts them from some platting and fencing rules when each grave is mapped or located by GPS. Buildings there are limited to winter storage and educational or devotional structures, and deeds must say so. Embalming is not needed for this kind of burial, and the FTC Funeral Rule bars a home from saying the law requires it when it does not. Check a license or file a complaint with the Vermont Office of Professional Regulation at 802-828-1188.

burial-costs-colorado.html: Family or home burial where allowed

Family or home burial where allowed: Colorado is among the states most open to family and home burial, and where it is possible it can remove cemetery fees altogether while still satisfying state rules; our home funeral guide covers the paperwork. Once a funeral home is involved, a clock starts. Under C.R.S. 12-135-106, the establishment must embalm, refrigerate, cremate, bury or entomb the remains within twenty-four hours of taking custody, so ask how that first day of care is billed.
funeral-costs-colorado.html: The $255 Social Security death payment goes only to an eligible surviving spouse or child, who applies by calling 1-800-772-1213 within two years of the death. The funeral bill itself is governed by C.R.S. 12-135-107: a Colorado establishment must hand over a written, itemized list of every service and item before you choose the funeral, cannot make you buy anything on it that the law does not require, and may label a charge a cash advance only when it is the same amount the family would pay the outside vendor directly.
funeral-costs-hawaii.html: The FTC Funeral Rule bars a Hawaii

Federal law already stops a Hawaii funeral home from claiming embalming is legally required when it is not, and its price list must say embalming is unnecessary outside certain special cases; ask any home that pushes embalming to cite the rule in writing. Hawaii adds its own price protection. HRS §441-22.6 requires every mortuary, cemetery or pre-need funeral authority to give a prospective buyer a current price list for written approval, with each item priced separately, and §441-22.5 bars charging more than the signed list unless you ask for an added item and approve its price.
cremation-costs-alabama.html: An Alabama provider offering direct cremation

An Alabama provider offering direct cremation must let you use an unfinished wood box or other alternative container instead of a casket (FTC Funeral Rule, 16 CFR 453.3(b)). State law spells out what that box must be: Code of Ala. §34-13-121(e) asks only for a combustible, closable, leak-resistant and rigid container labeled with the decedent's name and date of death. The same section lets the family member who signs the authorization witness the transport to the crematory, and a home that bars relatives from viewing the cremation must say so in writing before any contract is signed.
cremation-costs-pennsylvania.html: A Pennsylvania provider offering direct cremation

A Pennsylvania provider offering direct cremation must let you use an unfinished wood box or other alternative container instead of a casket (FTC Funeral Rule, 16 CFR 453.3(b)). Timing rules sit in the Board's regulations. 49 Pa. Code §13.212 allows a body to reach the crematory before the 24-hour mark only with explicit written instructions not to cremate early, backed by a signed receipt the funeral director keeps, and §13.184 bars a funeral home from holding remains more than 10 days in total without the Board's special permission.
funeral-costs-pennsylvania.html: The biggest lever is comparison shopping

Comparing two or three GPLs from different Pennsylvania providers line by line regularly saves $1,000 or more. Between December and March, ask cemeteries for frozen-ground pricing separately, because winter surcharges are common, and expect municipal, Catholic and Jewish cemeteries to come in $1,000 or more under private memorial parks; direct cremation, at $2,000, is the lowest-cost option in the state. Whatever you pick, 49 Pa. Code §13.204 makes the director sign a written agreement at the time of arrangements and before disposition, listing professional services, merchandise, facilities and equipment, itemizing each cash advance and giving the total, on a form that conforms to the FTC rule in 16 CFR Part 453.
cremation-costs-alaska.html: An Alaska provider offering direct cremation

Even the cheapest Alaska direct cremation lets you skip the casket: the provider must accept an unfinished wood box or other alternative container (FTC Funeral Rule, 16 CFR 453.3(b)). Paperwork sets the earliest date. Under AS 18.50.230, the death certificate has to be filed with the local registrar within three days and before final disposition, and the physician, advanced practice registered nurse or physician assistant must sign the medical certification within 24 hours, unless a medical examiner inquiry is required.
funeral-costs-alaska.html: To collect the one-time $255 from Social Security, an Alaska

Only a surviving spouse or eligible child can claim Social Security's one-time $255, by phoning 1-800-772-1213 within two years of the death. Alaska also leaves room for a simpler arrangement than a full funeral. AS 08.42.020(c) lets the state issue a permit to an unlicensed person to care for and dispose of bodies for pay when no embalming is involved, and AS 08.42.100 requires each funeral establishment to display its own location permit.

funeral-costs-louisiana.html: To collect the one-time $255 from Social Security, a Louisiana

Louisiana survivors claim the one-time $255 from Social Security by phone (1-800-772-1213); only a widow, widower or eligible child qualifies, and the deadline is two years. When none of them can give authorization, a district court judgment is required, which adds delay and legal cost.
burial-costs-nebraska.html: Work with independent funeral homes: Nebraska keeps a large

Work with independent funeral homes: ownership alone does not set the price; the itemized price list every Nebraska home must hand you does, so line those lists up item by item. Whichever home you choose takes on the paperwork. Neb. Rev. Stat. 71-605 makes the funeral director and embalmer in charge fill out the death certificate, and the attending physician, physician assistant or nurse practitioner must sign it electronically within twenty-four hours.
cremation-costs-wyoming.html: A Wyoming provider offering direct cremation

Wyoming families buying direct cremation do not need a casket; federal rules make the provider offer an unfinished wood box or another alternative container (FTC Funeral Rule, 16 CFR 453.3(b)). The permit comes first. Under W.S. 35-1-420, whoever first takes custody of the body obtains a burial-transit permit within seventy-two hours of death, and the local registrar may not issue a cremation permit until the death certificate has been filed.
burial-costs-iowa.html: Work with independent funeral homes: Iowa

Look past the funeral home for savings too: in Iowa the cemetery's own charges can be a large share of a burial bill, and state law makes the cemetery spell each of them out in advance. On the cemetery side, Iowa Code §523I.301 requires a cemetery to say before a sale whether opening and closing is included, to disclose current opening and closing prices if it is not, and to list every fee for interment or disinterment. Section 523I.303 bars a cemetery from shutting out the licensed funeral director you hired.
burial-costs-idaho.html: A growing number of Idaho cemeteries

Green burial sections, meaning a biodegradable container with no embalming and no vault, are offered by some Idaho cemeteries but not all, so check with the cemetery you are considering about whether it has a green section and how its prices compare; where none is close, some families buy a traditional plot and simply skip embalming. Many rural Idaho cemeteries are run by public districts. Idaho Code §27-101 declares cemetery upkeep a public purpose, and §27-121 lets a cemetery maintenance district levy up to 0.04% of taxable market value, which helps keep district plot prices low.
burial-costs-illinois.html: Work with independent funeral homes: a strong family-owned

Work with independent funeral homes: an Illinois home's ownership says little about its prices, so request the General Price List from each one you are considering and compare the same lines. Cemeteries carry duties of their own. 225 ILCS 411/20-5 requires a cemetery authority to publish its rules online (or send a copy within 5 days of a request) and to show and give you its current prices for interment, inurnment, entombment and disinterment, and it makes the cemetery responsible for opening and closing graves on its property.
funeral-costs-washington.html: Ask every Washington funeral home for its General Price List

Ask every Washington funeral home for its General Price List, which the FTC Funeral Rule requires it to hand you in person. RCW 18.39.195 goes further: a director must give accurate prices when you ask by phone, text or email, provide a written itemized statement before the service, and bill a "cash advanced" item only at the net amount actually paid.
burial-costs-missouri.html: Direct (immediate) burial, with no embalming, viewing or funeral-home ceremony, is normally the cheapest burial line on a Missouri price list, and the FTC Funeral Rule bars a handling fee when you bring your own casket. Eligible veterans pay nothing in a VA national cemetery for the grave, opening and closing, liner or marker. At an endowed care cemetery, part of the plot price is set aside by law: RSMo 214.320 sends at least 15% of each grave's sale price, or $20 if greater, into the care trust. Anyone visiting an abandoned family cemetery or private burying ground that is surrounded by private land has a right of reasonable access during reasonable hours under RSMo 214.132.
cremation-costs-massachusetts.html: Ask how long the Massachusetts crematory

Ask how long the Massachusetts crematory usually takes to return the ashes once the permit is issued, and whether the quote covers delivery or only pickup. Collect them promptly: under M.G.L. c.114 §43M, a funeral establishment holding remains that no next of kin claims within 12 months may have them interred in a common grave or niche or scattered in a designated cemetery area, though a veteran's remains must go to a veterans' cemetery.
burial-costs-minnesota.html: Work with independent funeral homes: Minnesota's

Work with independent funeral homes: whoever owns a Minnesota home, its prices show up on the General Price List, so get one from each home and compare matching items. Timing drives some charges. Minn. Stat. §149A.94 requires burial or another disposition within 14 calendar days, and a body not buried within 72 hours must be embalmed, refrigerated or packed in dry ice, with refrigeration capped at 14 days and dry ice at four.
funeral-costs-maryland.html: Ask every Maryland funeral home for its General Price List

Ask every Maryland funeral home for its General Price List; under the FTC Funeral Rule it must give you one in person. Prepaying is regulated by Md. Health Occ. §7-405: the contract must say whether it is guaranteed, and within 10 days the seller must deposit 100% of service payments, 80% of a casket or vault price, and all other goods payments in escrow or trust.
burial-costs-maryland.html: Plots, opening and closing, and vault rules are priced separately at Maryland cemeteries, and because the FTC Funeral Rule reaches funeral homes rather than most cemeteries, a written itemized list may not be mandatory; request one regardless. Baltimore National Cemetery is among the VA national cemeteries in the state. State law does fix the paperwork: under Md. Health-Gen. §4-215, the mortician must obtain a burial-transit permit within 72 hours of death, no cemetery may accept a body without one, and the cemetery writes the lot and space number on the permit and files it within 10 days.
Because the Funeral Consumers Alliance does not count Maryland

Maryland is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance list of nine states that require a funeral director, so a family may handle a burial itself, provided it has the burial permit and follows the cemetery's own rules for the grave.
Compare at least two Maryland cemeteries
Price the cemetery and the funeral home separately in Maryland: the plot, grave opening and marker come from the cemetery, so get at least two quotes for each.
If the person served, ask Crownsville Veterans Cemetery
For a veteran, call Crownsville Veterans Cemetery first and ask which documents it wants; the DD214 discharge record is normally one of them.
Report a funeral home that misprices a burial to the board at 410-764-4792
A Maryland funeral home that misstates burial prices can be reported to the state board at 410-764-4792.
cremation-costs-nebraska.html: Nebraska scattering rules depend on the specific location, and many families choose a columbarium niche, urn burial or keepsake jewelry instead. Settle the choice early. Under Neb. Rev. Stat. 71-1382, delivering the ashes to the authorizing agent counts as final disposition, and if no one claims or directs them within sixty days of cremation, the crematory or funeral home may dispose of them after a reasonable attempt to make contact.
cremation-costs-nevada.html: Choose a flat-rate direct cremation provider

Choose a direct cremation provider on what the price covers: compare each Nevada provider's direct cremation line, from transport and the container to the permit and any certified death certificates, and weigh what is included against the provider's reputation. State law sets handling standards for all of them. Under NRS 451.675, an unembalmed body may be held no longer than 24 hours unless the holding room is refrigerated, and NRS 451.690 requires a signed receipt at pickup and a sealed, tracked package if the ashes are shipped.
burial-costs-kansas.html: Green burial sections, which take a biodegradable container and skip embalming and the vault, are spreading across Kansas cemeteries and usually total less than a conventional burial; where no such ground is close, some Kansas families pick a hybrid, a regular plot with no embalming. Part of any lot price is earmarked by statute. K.S.A. 17-1301c defines the share a cemetery corporation must put into its permanent maintenance fund as 15% of a burial lot's purchase price with a $25 floor, 10% (at least $100) of a community mausoleum crypt and 5% (at least $50) of a garden mausoleum crypt or niche.
burial-costs-arizona.html: Arizona's cheapest burial line is usually direct (immediate) burial, since no embalming, viewing or funeral-home ceremony is involved, and a casket bought elsewhere cannot draw a handling fee under the FTC Funeral Rule. Qualifying veterans pay nothing at a VA national cemetery for the plot, the opening and closing, or the headstone. If you are offered a bargain casket, know the limits in A.R.S. § 32-1365. A casket that already held a body may not be used for another burial, and a former rental casket may be sold only with written disclosure and a new pillow and mattress.
Because the Funeral Consumers Alliance does not count Arizona

Arizona is missing from the Funeral Consumers Alliance count of nine states that insist on a funeral director, which leaves an Arizona family free to arrange a burial on its own once the burial permit is issued, subject to the cemetery's rules.
Compare at least two Arizona cemeteries
In Arizona the cemetery prices the plot, opening and marker separately from the funeral home, so collect two or more quotes on each side.
If the person served, ask National Memorial Cemetery of Arizona
Veterans' families should check with National Memorial Cemetery of Arizona about the records it needs before the service, starting with the DD214.
Report a funeral home that misprices a burial to the board at 602-364-2079
Pricing complaints about an Arizona funeral home go to the state board, 602-364-2079.
cremation-costs-oklahoma.html: Plenty of Oklahoma families want cremation and a traditional viewing too. That combination runs about $5,000 here, compared with the $1,400 direct cremation minimum, and it is most popular in Oklahoma City and Tulsa. Oklahoma has long trailed the national cremation rate; this site rounds the state figure to about 45%, while NFDA projected 63.4% nationally for 2025. Once cremation is decided but a visitation still matters, get the cremation-with-service package priced on its own, because Oklahoma funeral homes often quote it very differently from direct cremation, and ask about renting a ceremonial casket instead of buying one that will be cremated. If relatives hope to share the ashes, plan for it in writing: under 59 O.S. § 396.29, cremated remains may not be divided or separated without the authorizing agent's prior written consent.
cremation-costs-washington.html: Cremation pricing in Washington is simpler

Cremation in Washington costs less than burial, yet providers can still be thousands of dollars apart. In Washington, direct cremation starts around $2,100 while cremation with a full service averages $6,800, a gap of $4,700. Below we cover what each price tier includes and how a 76% cremation rate shapes the market. One cost a Washington family can usually avoid is a cemetery niche, since RCW 68.50.130 lets cremated remains be placed on private property with the owner's consent, or on public lands or waters with approval from the agency in charge.
burial-costs-north-dakota.html: Burial costs in North Dakota are shaped

A North Dakota burial arrives as three bills: about $6,700 for the funeral home's services, plot and interment charges at the cemetery that start near $3,000, and a headstone or marker at $500–$5,000. The state also sets a deadline. Under N.D.C.C. § 23-06-04, the body must be disposed of within eight days of death unless an exception applies, such as a longer-hold permit from the local health officer. Before buying a plot, check the deed history too: § 23-06-21.1 lets a cemetery start proceedings to take back a deeded space that has gone unused for burial for more than sixty years.
burial-costs-michigan.html: Request itemized pricing from every provider

Request itemized pricing from every provider: a General Price List is mandatory for Michigan funeral homes. Cemeteries have no such duty, but most around Michigan will hand over an itemized price sheet when you ask for that rather than a "package." Timing matters as well, because under MCL 333.2848 the funeral director who first takes custody must obtain the authorization for final disposition within 72 hours of the death, on a state form signed by the local or state registrar.
burial-costs-florida.html: Church and family cemeteries still sit beside commercial ones across much of Florida, and congregations often price their sections under the market. Holding a church or family plot in Florida could save more than $1,440 against a private cemetery (our estimate), and state law permits family burial plots on private land, subject to local rules. Older grounds have a safety net as well: under Fla. Stat. § 497.284, a county or city may step in to maintain and secure an abandoned cemetery, or one left unmaintained for more than 6 months, after notice to the state department.
burial-costs-south-carolina.html: Plot, opening and closing, and any vault or liner requirement are priced cemetery by cemetery in South Carolina, and since the FTC Funeral Rule reaches funeral homes rather than most cemeteries, an itemized list may not be owed; ask for it all the same. Beaufort National Cemetery and Florence National Cemetery Annex are among the VA national cemeteries in the state. For a grave in an old family plot that now sits on someone else's land, S.C. Code § 27-43-310 obliges the landowner to allow ingress and egress to descendants, plot owners and people lawfully taking part in a burial, for purposes such as visiting and maintaining the graves.
burial-costs-nevada.html: Nevada does not require a funeral director for a burial. It is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance's list of nine states that do, so families here may deal straight with the cemetery over the grave space, its opening and what kind of container it takes. Expect a maintenance charge on the plot itself, because NRS 452.070 lets a cemetery authority adopt care and maintenance plans and collect reasonable sums from later plot purchasers to fund them.
A traditional burial in Nevada costs

A traditional burial in Nevada costs approximately $8,000 for the funeral service plus a cemetery plot that commonly falls in the $4,200 to $8,000 range in metropolitan areas. When you add a burial vault ($1,520), opening and closing fees ($1,900), casket ($2,400), and headstone ($500-$5,000), the Nevada total typically ranges from $18,120 to $22,620. A burial permit is required before cemetery burial can proceed, and the cemetery owner must keep the grounds orderly, including mowing grass at least monthly in the growing season, a duty the county commissioners, the district attorney or a relative of anyone buried there can enforce (NRS 452.030).
cremation-costs-rhode-island.html: A full-service cremation in Rhode Island means visitation and a ceremony first, with cremation taking the place of burial; a memorial after cremation is just as common and leaves the venue and date open. Among the Rhode Island prices above, only direct cremation, at $2,200, leaves the service out. The paperwork deadline is separate from the cremation wait: R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-3-18(a) has the funeral director who first takes custody prepare the burial-transit permit within seven calendar days of death and before final disposition.
cremation-costs-florida.html: Florida is not among the states that, by the Funeral Consumers Alliance's tally of nine, insist on a funeral director. In practice, though, a Florida crematory still waits for three documents: the death certificate, the cremation permit and a signed authorization from the next of kin. Decide early what happens to the ashes, too: Fla. Stat. § 497.607 requires a signed declaration of intent for the remains at the arrangement, has the cremation done within 48 hours of a time agreed in writing, and treats cremated remains as not property, so dividing them needs the legally authorized person's consent.
cremation-costs-new-mexico.html: When no estate exists, a New Mexico county may put up to $1,000 toward cremating an unclaimed person (NMSA § 24-13-3), though not until 14 days after death. (Source: NMSA §§ 24-13-1, 24-13-3.) Against the $1,500 direct cremation estimate above, the $255 Social Security lump sum for an eligible spouse or child is only a partial offset. Board rules also bar placing two bodies in one retort without written consent from each authorizing agent, and no crematory has to do it even with consent (16.64.10.8 NMAC).
cremation-costs-south-dakota.html: A South Dakota county pays for an indigent cremation

If relatives cannot pay, the South Dakota county covers an indigent cremation (SDCL 28-17-1) and holds a lien on what the deceased owned. (Source: SDCL 28-17-1; SDCL ch. 28-14.) When everyone with the duty fails to act, it falls to the county of legal residence, or the county where the body was found, which then has a preferred claim on the estate for the actual cost (SDCL 34-26-17). Social Security's $255 death payment to a qualifying spouse or child pays just a slice of the $1,500 direct cremation figure above.
cremation-costs-new-hampshire.html: Ask about current turnaround: New Hampshire bars cremation until 48 hours after death and requires the medical examiner's certificate (RSA 325-A:18); beyond that, timing varies, so ask the provider for a written estimate. Collect the ashes promptly, since a New Hampshire crematory may dispose of unclaimed remains 60 days after cremation once it has tried to reach the authorizing agent (RSA 325-A:27).

cremation-costs-maryland.html: Maryland's $650 Burial Assistance payment can go toward a cremation as long as the funeral cost stays at or under $2,500, and it cannot reimburse bills already paid (COMAR 07.03.20.03). (Source: COMAR 07.03.20.03.) The $255 Social Security death payment to a qualifying Maryland spouse or child would cover only part of the $2,200 direct cremation estimate above. Keep the casket off the bill too: nobody in Maryland may insist that a cremation be done in a casket, though a simple container may be required (Md. Health-Gen. § 5-505).

Ask about current turnaround: Maryland requires at least 12 hours between death and cremation (Md. Health-Gen. § 5-503); after that, how long it takes depends on the crematory's schedule, so get its estimate in writing.
cremation-costs-colorado.html: Colorado is not among the nine states

A Colorado family can arrange cremation without a funeral director (the Funeral Consumers Alliance omits Colorado from its nine-state list), but the crematory still wants the death certificate, the cremation permit and the next of kin's signed authorization. It must also give a receipt signed by both sides when the body is delivered and again when the ashes are released, and keep those receipts and a permanent cremation record for at least five years (C.R.S. 12-135-305).
burial-costs-alaska.html: Alaska does not require a funeral director for a burial

No funeral director is needed for an Alaska burial (the Funeral Consumers Alliance does not put Alaska among its nine states), so the family can settle the plot, the grave opening and the accepted container with the cemetery itself. Where filing the death certificate first would cause undue hardship, state regulations may allow the burial-transit permit to issue before that certificate is filed (AS 18.50.260).
burial-costs-connecticut.html: A burial in Connecticut cannot be handled entirely by the family

Connecticut families cannot do every step of a burial themselves. The Funeral Consumers Alliance reads Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 7-62b, 7-65a and 7-69 as requiring a licensed funeral director to file the death certificate, move the body and get the disposition permit, and the grave itself is opened and closed by the Connecticut cemetery.
If a Connecticut funeral home gives you misleading burial prices, you can complain to the state at 860-509-7603 at no cost.

Help for a family without money depends on Shelby County

Help for a family without money depends on Shelby County. Tennessee lets each county's legislative body decide whether it will pay for the burial or cremation of a poor person, and any claim must come with a sworn statement of the cost and of the lack of other means (Tenn. Code Ann. § 5-9-101(4); § 5-9-311). Ask the Shelby County mayor's office how the county handles this before you commit to a funeral home. Social Security's $255 death payment, limited to a qualifying spouse or child, covers only a sliver of the $7,035 Tennessee average in the table. Tennessee does set one floor: when the medical examiner cannot release a body to relatives, the body must be decently buried or cremated, with the cost taken from property found with it or, failing that, paid from the county treasury (Tenn. Att'y Gen. Op. 18-13, citing Tenn. Code Ann. § 38-5-118).
burial-costs-indiana.html: In Indiana the person in charge of the burial must get a permit

In Indiana the person in charge of the burial must get a permit for disposition from the local health officer of the county where the death happened, and must have it before the burial and before the body leaves that county. The health officer issues it once the death certificate has been properly completed (IC 16-37-3-10 and -11; checked October 29, 2026). A family that hopes to bury on its own land should ask the county or town first: the state's Division of Historic Preservation and Archaeology does not create cemeteries and sends anyone planning a family cemetery to local government, with IC 23-14 as the governing law. Once a cemetery exists on private land, the parcel it sits on can be reclassified as cemetery land and assessed at $1 an acre (IC 6-1.1-6.8), and anyone later selling that property must record the deed with CEMETERY in bold capitals at the bottom (IC 14-21-3), so the choice follows the land for good (Indiana DNR cemetery laws).
